Description

In resting cells RAF kinases (ARAF, BRAF, RAF1) sit in the cytoplasm as monomers held inactive by a 14-3-3 dimer, which binds two phosphoserines flanking the kinase domain (S365 and S729 in BRAF, S259 and S621 in RAF1) and hides the membrane-binding cysteine-rich domain [9]. GTP-loaded RAS binds the RAS-binding domain of RAF and brings it to the plasma membrane, and membrane recruitment is what activates RAF [1-4]. There a phosphatase made of SHOC2, the catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1C) and GTP-loaded MRAS removes the N-terminal inhibitory phosphate, which frees that end of RAF from 14-3-3 [5-8]. Two such RAF molecules then form a back-to-back dimer, a single 14-3-3 dimer bridging their C-terminal phosphoserines and the second 14-3-3 dimer leaving. Dimerisation drives the catalytic activity of RAF, and BRAF and RAF1 form heterodimers as well as homodimers [9-12]. How RAS binding opens the autoinhibited monomer in detail still differs between structural studies.
